questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The use of english as the language of teaching and in society in general.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Quite easy

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was quite a lot of information through mails, and many events for newcoming exchangers.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There were quite a few options including different halls and residents - I chose to apply for a different halls and were accepted into my first priority.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: The hall I got accepted into had an obligatory mealplan consisting of breakfast and dinner 6 days a week. Otherwise there were many restaurants at campus and close by. In the hall there was also a kitchen with basic necessities such a sink, stovetop, airfryer and fridge that the blocks had to share. So possible to cook simple stuff.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: That exchangers (at the time I came) were mostly accepted into campus housing, but that it is very competitive and sought after by the local students. Therefore to stay more than one semester there are a lot of requirements and kind of a point system where the people with most points get to stay for the next semesters. But normaly exchangers are exempted from this. Othewise one has to choose an accomodation that fits you - there are many different kinds where the focus of social life could be either sports, music, partying or more acedemic things. So in general dont stress.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It is the same as the locals and therefore depending on what you are willing to pay and what kind of housing you like yiu will be equal to the local students. So not worse or better. The more epxensive housing have better food and facilities, but the cheaper are nice aswell if you don't mind older facilities and houses.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: When you get accepted by KU and register and apply, you are given a lot of step by step material that you are guided by. You first apply for getting accepted by the host university by choosing and applying to different courses that you would like to have. Acceptance of these courses depends on your grades, and the more popular courses (economy, architecture etc) will get filled by the people with the higest average. You have to apply for 8 courses, and to get accepted into the host university you have to get into at least 3 of the courses. It can be nerverecking since you dont know what your chances are  - but remeber that whatever courses you are allocated when registering, you can always change when your have arrived. The first 2-3 weeks of the semester is kind of an introduction to the courses and you can change if it isn't something you like (based on availablity of other courses ofc.) But in general it seems more strict than it is even though the system is quite flexible.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: A lot of step by step guides and emails. Even online zoom seminars that guide you through the process. The website is also quite helpful.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was quite succesful and out of my top 4 choices I got into 3 of them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Dont stress in choosing exactly the courses that you want in the registration and first application, you can always change your courses later if you are unsure if you like them or not. The forst couple of weeks there is a possibilty to switch your courses. So no stress. The system is more flexible than it seems.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took level 3000 and level 1000 courses which is the same as third and first year BA courses respectively. Third year courses were the courses that were a part of my field (geography), and the other where introductionary courses to other fields of study that I found interesting (History and sociology)

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Similar acedemic level, yet depending on field of study most grades are a mix of exams, participation, quizzes, mid-terms and assignments which means that the workload throughout the semester can be quite high (not neccesarily hard, just a lot to do all the time)

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Land below the winds: Introduction to Southeast Aisa
- Nationbuilding in Malaysia and Singapore
- Aquarian, Riprarian and Coastal Ecosystems
- Cities and Regions: Planning for change

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed the introduction to southeast asia course since its a historical and cultural introduction to the region you will be living in (and probably also travel a lot in). And the proffesors a very good.

questions.answer: Visa applications

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Food in hawker centers and food courts are mostly cheaper than expected, but supermarkets are wuite expensive (same as in Denmark I would say). Transport is very cheap and drinks (coffes, teas and juices) are cheap. Everything else is quite expensive and you shouldn't expect stores and malls to be cheaper than in DK

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is so much you can do and join, but be reminded that you might be cut out of fx sports teams after a couple of months because you are only there for one semester and they prefer people to be there for a year.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: A lot. All kinds of sports, religious activites, games, music etc. The amount of clubs and groups seems unlimited.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed the many seminars that profs and students would organize - with evening lectures and workshops about a wide range of themes.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I recomnend getting of campus - which sounds easy to do - but its so easy to just end up spending all your time on campus. Go out, the museums are free for students and parks are everywhere.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy since everything was in english.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Singaporeans are BUSY. All the time. They dont sleep a lot, so expect people to be awake to quite late and always be busy with stuff (studying, clubs, groups etc) so they quickly end up only really socialising with people from thier groups and clubs. Remember that most also go home in the weekend to be with family, so socializing mostly happens throughout the weekdays

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Singaporeans are really sweet in firsthand encounters but because they are so busy always its hard to get to know them.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The food and all the activities that there is around the city (cultural festivals, musuems etc)

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Remember it humid and hot outside, but inside its freezing because of the AC. 
2) Dont stress with registration - it looks strict and hard but its quite flexible. Relax.
3) Enjoy the diversity of food and drinks (remember to include food in the budget eventhough you have mealplans)

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Even though the uni is asian and you might have some expectation of it being hard and competetive - its much more relaxed in reality, eventhough workload is a lot (but not necesarily hard)

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: All the things I learned about Asia

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The big workload and how to get into a healthy routine were school didn't take up most of my time.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
